data.title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp announces half-price fares for ‘Thank You Day’ on October 24
data.description:
Hong Kong’s rail operator will offer half-price fares across its network on October 24, as part of a “Thank You Day”.
The MTR Corporation said discounts would apply to Octopus and JoyYou card users on its railway, Light Rail and bus services in the northwestern New Territories, as well as to QR code ticket holders on the heavy rail network.
Cross-border journeys to and from Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau stations on the East Rail line will also be covered.
Passengers can combine the half-price discount with interchange and fare saver discounts, a 25 per cent discount on connecting journeys under the monthly pass and the government’s HK$2 (25 US cents) fare concession scheme for elderly passengers and eligible people with disabilities.

The discount will not apply to East Rail first class, the Airport Express, MTR feeder bus services, single-journey tickets, contactless card payments or the Hong Kong section of the high-speed rail.
“The corporation will deploy additional staff at MTR stations to assist passengers and closely monitor train and station operations to suitably adjust train service and manpower arrangements when necessary,” it said.
The promotional day falls under the MTR’s service performance rebate arrangement, part of the fare adjustment mechanism, which offers discounted fares on a designated Saturday or Sunday once the rebate fund reaches HK$25 million.
Last year, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan confirmed that the corporation had been fined HK$19.2 million over a five-hour disruption on the Tseung Kwan O line in May, with the penalty allocated to passenger rebates.

data.title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan to set goals, not alter economic system: John Lee
data.description:
Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will include both binding and aspirational targets, the city’s leader has said, stressing that the long-term blueprint does not signal a move towards a planned economy.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also revealed on Tuesday that the plan, which will be unveiled alongside his annual policy address the following day, would feature a blue cover symbolising “blue skies”, openness, progress and steadiness.
“There will be indicators which are binding and indicators which are anticipatory … There are things we must do and they are binding on the government particularly,” Lee told the media ahead of the top decision-making Executive Council meeting.
“And there are things we want to do very much, but we need everybody to facilitate. The government will lead, and also the government will coordinate resources, make the right policies, and everybody has to play their part in order to achieve the best result.”
But he stopped short of saying whether specific indicators would be set for major initiatives such as the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
Lee also reiterated that the plan would not alter Hong Kong’s economic system.
“I want to make it very clear: the five-year plan is not a planned economy. It is a plan which tells us where the strategic directions are, where we are heading and which are the priority areas,” Lee said.
“It is a blueprint for us to implement in five years’ time. So when we each year roll out policies, we also have to ascertain priorities so that at the end of five years we will reach certain goals.”
Lee said the theme of his fifth and final policy address of his current term would be: “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era; Driving Reform and Boosting Development; Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihood”.

He said the document would retain its green cover, symbolising policy continuity, vibrancy and hope. It would also carry special significance as the first policy address to follow the announcement of the five-year plan.
“It means that we adopt a long-term perspective through the five-year plan to map out Hong Kong’s overall development, advance reforms, promote growth and create opportunities,” Lee said.
“[We will] ensure that the benefits of economic development are shared with the public, and that we embrace the future.”
Lee is scheduled to present both documents to the Legislative Council on Wednesday morning. He said they contained more than 100,000 words in total and that he would spend two to three hours outlining their key points.
The government had also prepared a summary to help the public understand the relationship between the two documents and the measures they contained, Lee added.
Authorities have said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan aims to align the city’s development more closely with the national blueprint for 2026-2030, while providing strategic direction for the years ahead.
The plan will outline the city’s vision for the metropolis, the advancement of innovation and technology, and the development of the finance, shipping and trading sectors.
The policy address will serve as a progress report on the implementation of the plan, setting out policies and advancing its direction in response to the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments.
The government earlier concluded a months-long public consultation on both documents. It held two town hall meetings attended by more than 200 residents and district representatives, and received more than 17,000 submissions on the five-year plan and 11,000 on the policy address.

data.title: Forms Syntron draws Hong Kong’s next-gen tycoons in HK$940 million IPO
data.description:
Hong Kong’s younger generation of tycoons is becoming increasingly active in the city’s initial public offering market through family offices and private investments. But their investments extend beyond the property and traditional financial sectors associated with their predecessors, into technology and digital finance.
Prominent business leaders Cheng Chi-heng of New World Development and Peter Lee Ka-kit of Henderson Land participated as cornerstone investors in Shenzhen Forms Syntron Information’s HK$940 million (US$119.8 million) Hong Kong listing, according to the company’s official filing on Monday.
In exchange for guaranteed share allocations and a mandatory commitment to hold the stocks for at least six months, Cheng and Lee agreed to buy HK$40 million and HK$39.6 million worth of shares, respectively. They were joined by private investment firm Thalassa Capital and Hong Kong-listed LCD manufacturer Yeebo International Holdings.
Lee has been particularly active in Hong Kong’s IPO market in recent years. Through his wholly-owned private investment vehicle, he has served as a cornerstone investor in several high-profile debuts, including XtalPi in 2024 – the first specialist technology company to list under Hong Kong’s Chapter 18C rules designed for innovative firms in hi-tech industries.
As the city’s broader IPO market stages a robust recovery in 2026 – with total funds raised surpassing HK$340 billion in the first eight months – tycoons and family offices are drawing renewed market attention.
Forms Syntron said it met these high-profile investors through business connections, introductions by corporate partners and global offering underwriters during its regular business and investment activities.

The financial technology service provider, which caters to the banking industry, has started taking investor orders for its Hong Kong listing and expects its trading debut on September 22. It is offering 58.9 million shares at a maximum price of HK$16 each, according to its listing document. The price marks a 40 per cent discount compared with the 23.02 yuan (US$3.43) closing price of its Shenzhen-listed shares on Friday.
The company plans to channel the capital raised into research and development, operational capabilities over the next three to five years, international sales expansion across mainland China and overseas markets, and potential strategic technology acquisitions.
Although headquartered in mainland China and already listed in the A-share market, Forms Syntron has strong ties to Hong Kong. Founder and chairman Chow Chi Kwan grew up and was educated in the city, earning a bachelor’s degree in social science from the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 1995. He also serves as a non-official member of Hong Kong’s Digital Economy Development Committee.
Founded in 2003, Forms Syntron provides fintech software development, consulting and systems integration services to banks, regulatory authorities and financial institutions across mainland China and Hong Kong, supporting their digital transformation.
The Hong Kong market now accounts for more than 80 per cent of the company’s total revenue. Its client base mainly comprises financial institutions and non-bank financial firms, with its top five customers contributing 89.1 per cent of revenue in 2025.
The company recorded revenue of 630 million yuan (US$93.9 million) last year, down from 740 million yuan in 2024. Full-year net profit rose 10.3 per cent year on year to 74 million yuan. The company won 221 new projects in 2025, compared with 297 in 2024.

data.title: Data from Greater Bay Area residents to help improve healthcare policy: GSK
data.description:
British pharmaceutical company GSK is turning to patient data gathered from the 88 million residents of the Greater Bay Area’s 11 cities to speed up drug development in vaccines and cancer care, as officials push for closer cross-border medical cooperation.
GSK Hong Kong and Macau general manager Nicholas Teo said patient data was very important because it could form “supplementary evidence” to support regulatory filings and potential label expansions, and also help to “discover benefits other than the medication itself”.
Vaccines were one example, Teo said last week. While their effectiveness against target diseases such as flu, shingles and respiratory syncytial virus was well established, he said researchers were increasingly studying potential benefits relating to cardiovascular health and neurological outcomes, which might help generate additional evidence and insights for future healthcare decision-making.
Teo said GSK’s expertise lay in vaccination and disease prevention, citing shingles and respiratory syncytial virus as key areas, with the viral liver infection hepatitis B another area of focus. He added that GSK also had a growing oncology and haematology portfolio.
The bay area is a government scheme aimed at integrating Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in mainland China’s Guangdong province into a single economic and business hub. Their combined gross domestic product last year was more than US$2.23 trillion, according to official data.
GSK signed a memorandum of understanding in September last year with the University of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute on a study to examine the long-term health effects of the shingles vaccine.
Teo said GSK would provide financial sponsorship for the HKU-led study and was also investing in shared data infrastructure. The company could access patient data through the partnership, such as data coming from hospitals and government agencies, but pharmaceutical companies did not have direct access to it on their own, he added.
The institute, based in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and set up by the Hong Kong government, enables the free exchange of researchers and data between the two cities.
Better decisions are made after we have better data
Nicholas Teo, GSK Hong Kong and Macau
The director of its real-world study and application centre, Cheung Ching-lung, said at the Hong Kong International Biotechnology Conference and Exhibition on Thursday that the institute aimed to use real-world data to drive evidence-based decision-making through global collaboration.
He said real-world data was patient data gathered during routine clinical practice at hospitals and clinics.
HKU pharmacy professor Ian Wong said at the conference that cross-border research required “infrastructure that’s safe enough” as the first pillar, alongside government regulation, ethics and public education, before real-world data could be used effectively.
Raphael Yeung, a senior pharmacist at Hong Kong’s Drug Office, said the city had multiple regulatory safeguards in place, including the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance.
Teo said the value of data ultimately came down to better outcomes and better policy.
“Better decisions are made after we have better data,” he said. “If we have data that tells you a certain medication or vaccine benefits a particular population, the government can take a decision on whether to make it available, subsidise it, or improve access.”
Teo added that GSK wanted to help prove that the cross-border data pipeline could work at scale.
“We hope to be part of potential pilot studies or collaborations that will prove this data flow is safe, secure and high quality between Hong Kong and mainland China,” he said.

data.title: Hong Kong leader vows accountability over faulty lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities will hold construction firms and government personnel accountable for faulty lift installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block, the city’s leader has said, as he tasked the Development Bureau with submitting a report within a month.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday that he had instructed the bureau, which had given him a preliminary briefing, to “thoroughly investigate the matter and report within a month”.
“We will pursue accountability, including contractors, subcontractors, engineering personnel and professionals. And if there are government personnel involved, we will pursue their accountability as well,” he said ahead of his meeting with the Executive Council. “We also need to identify where and whether the system has any inadequacies and rectify them.
“To consider what further action we will do, we must first find very clearly about what happened, where are the inadequacies, and whether any person who should be held accountable, we should pursue their accountability. After we have found out the facts, then we will decide what further steps we shall take.”

Lee’s comments came a month after defective work at the hospital – the largest on Hong Kong Island – came under scrutiny, with 24 of the 28 lifts in its new 34-storey clinical block deemed unfit for use.
Sources previously told the South China Morning Post that Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department who oversaw the development, had been asked to resign and left her post over the scandal.
The department denied that there had been any “forced resignation”, saying Li had quit for “personal reasons” after giving three months’ notice.
Lee did not directly address the SCMP’s questions about whether the resignation would affect the investigation and why the government had not invoked its “Heads of Department Accountability System”, proposed in his policy address last year to improve governance.
He stressed that medical services were important to the public and that the new block should open as soon as possible.
Widespread installation defects, revealed last month, have delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, raising serious concerns over project oversight and civil service accountability.

data.title: In Focus|Cast out: why China’s young workers see sacking saga as sign of unsettling timesThe outlook for China’s young jobseekers could worsen further, after an ugly fallout from Xingyu’s mass dismiss
data.description:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.
Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.
The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.
They could either resign “voluntarily” and receive half a month’s salary, or stay and be reassigned from office-based technical roles to factory-floor work, including tightening screws.
According to the firm, 107 chose the former option. But the uproar that ensued has placed the company firmly in the centre of a media firestorm, with Communist Party news organ People’s Daily calling the move “a blatant trampling of social trust” in a commentary late last month.
The extensive public attention the incident aroused stood as a tangible reflection of corporate workforce contraction, youth employment pressure and growing incidents of labour disputes, phenomena occurring within a broader slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy, analysts said.
While neither the firm nor local authorities specified any violation of labour law by the short-term manoeuvre, which coincided with its application for a listing in Hong Kong, its adverse effects were evident, the analysts warned.
“The company’s planned Hong Kong listing is very likely to be blocked, because the negative impact is simply too damaging,” said Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing.
As for the employment of fresh graduates – an increasingly sensitive issue for Beijing amid a tough job market – “the fact that this incident has escalated to such a degree is also highly unfavourable. Big companies will become very cautious in their future hiring”, he said.
According to its statement, Xingyu had recruited more than 400 college graduates through campus hiring last autumn and this spring, while 372 formally joined the company in July.


About one month into their employment, the company’s human resources department conducted one-on-one meetings with each of them, presenting the binary choice. The decision resulted from a workforce optimisation plan “based on the company’s order pipeline and staffing needs”, it said.
The move sparked backlash from many former employees, who complained to domestic media that after being dismissed, they lost their status as fresh graduates and could only re-enter the job market as social hires with a termination record on their résumés.
Within China’s institutional framework, losing this status stripped them of many competitive job-seeking advantages.
The company and the municipal human resources bureau of Changzhou, where Xingyu is based, have so far arranged for 71 of those dismissed to join new employers, while an additional 22 passed interviews and received offer letters.
The remainder were either undertaking interviews or planning to pursue postgraduate studies, Xingyu said last week.
Previously, both the firm and the bureau responded with apologies and explanations over the incident but failed to quell widespread public scepticism.
On August 25, the bureau confirmed the controversial lay-off – after media reports went viral – noting that the negotiation process was “overly rigid and simplistic, lacking full and effective communication”.
Two days later, the firm issued a public apology, acknowledging “managerial errors in decision-making” and offering a package of remedies including three months’ worth of job-seeking living allowances, free dormitory accommodation and an additional six months’ salary compensation for those who remained unemployed.
At its half-year performance briefing on September 2, the company’s chairwoman and general manager, Zhou Xiaoping, apologised and said the company was “properly implementing remedial measures” under government guidance.
According to its earnings results, Xingyu posted revenue of 6.88 billion yuan (US$1 billion) in the first half of the year, up 1.87 per cent, year on year, with a profit of about 712 million yuan, down 7.78 per cent, year on year.
Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard
Nie Riming, Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law
Its 2025 sales figures showed that it held an 11.6 per cent share of China’s automotive lighting market, ranking first in the country, and accounted for 4.6 per cent of the global market share, ranking seventh.
Nie Riming, a researcher at the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law, said the broader lacklustre job market was primarily why this incident generated such a huge response.
“Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard,” he said.
Another record-breaking army of university graduates – an estimated 12.7 million students – entered China’s job market this summer, up about 4 per cent from last year, according to official data. The youth jobless rate – covering those aged 16 to 24, excluding students – climbed to 17.9 per cent in July from 14.9 per cent in the previous month.
Nie noted that Xingyu’s immediate cash compensation alone could compare favourably with statutory minimums in Germany, where labour protections are generally stronger.
While China has relatively high-standard labour laws on paper, enforcement and compliance are uneven, especially among smaller firms, he said. Against this backdrop, listed companies like Xingyu – along with foreign-invested firms and state-owned enterprises – remain the primary sources of higher-quality jobs in China.
However, these relatively “well-behaved” companies had been steadily reducing their headcount in recent years, and after this incident, such formal, regulated positions were likely to become even more scarce, he added.
“For companies going forward, they will become increasingly cautious when hiring for compliant, formal positions,” he said.
“They will lean more towards non-standard employment arrangements – such as outsourcing and dispatching – to offload their staffing responsibilities. That, in turn, would further reduce formal direct hiring and reinforce labour-market dualisation.”
The most contentious issue remains fresh graduate status, as many recruitment policies, including those for civil service admissions, favour fresh graduates, he said.


“The way graduates are regulated has yet to align with the job market, and this disconnect must be resolved before it causes further frustration,” he urged.
As the economic slowdown persists in China, lay-offs have become a recurring theme in the workplace, and labour disputes are on the rise.
Labour dispute mediation and arbitration bodies at all levels handled 4.54 million cases nationwide in 2025 – a 7 per cent increase from 2024, following a 10 per cent rise over 2023, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security’s annual statistical bulletin.
Meanwhile, Xingyu’s lay-off controversy emerged after it refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July, sparking market speculation that it was a short-term tactic to pad the company’s research workforce and make it look stronger for its listing ambitions.
Among the dismissed employees, about two-thirds held bachelor’s degrees, while the remainder held master’s degrees. The majority were assigned to research and development roles, as well as manufacturing and production positions, while a smaller number were allocated functional support roles, according to last week’s statement.
However, legal experts and academics considered it unlikely that this was the company’s primary intention, given that such a move would offer limited substantive gain while exposing it to significant compliance and reputational risks.
Such risks may soon materialise, such as hindering its listing progress, said Zhao Zhanling, a commercial lawyer from Beijing-based Javy Law Firm.
“The stock exchange and its advisers are likely to demand clarifications on the mass lay-offs, labour law compliance and internal control mechanisms,” he said. “Adverse media coverage may also invite regulatory questions, causing delays – though not necessarily scuttling the IPO altogether.”
The Shanghai Stock Exchange website showed that it issued a regulatory work letter to Xingyu on Wednesday, specifying regulatory requirements regarding the company’s “relevant matters”, without providing further details.
The saga could also lead to a loss of business opportunities, according to Tang, the Beijing researcher.
“It is possible that its international clients would respond positively to public outcry,” he said, “but that does not mean they would punish Xingyu – they may downgrade its supplier tier ... or impose more stringent supply conditions.”
Volkswagen China said earlier this month that it had initiated an investigation into the matter following intense media coverage.

data.title: ‘I just need an answer’: widow haunted by husband’s shooting seeks inquest
data.description:
Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held.
On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home.
Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors.
Little did Mrs Li, who preferred to be identified by her spouse’s surname, expect that the day would end in tragedy.
Police said an officer eventually shot the man at a distance of 1.5 metres (4.9 feet) after he allegedly ignored repeated warnings during a 30-second stand-off and attempted to attack them.
Now, all she wants is for a death inquest to be held as soon as possible to bring closure to herself and her husband, to whom she had been married for 10 years.
“I need no sympathy or pity. I just need an answer and hope to prevent this tragedy from happening again,” she said.
“It’s been two years, yet there is still no news. I’m anxious that this matter will just be left unsettled, and my husband’s death went unexplained.”
The then commissioner of police Raymond Siu Chak-yee defended the officer’s decision to shoot the man because he followed the guidelines on firearms use.
Siu said police would submit a death investigation report to the Coroner’s Court and “recommend the court hold a death inquest as soon as possible”.
But Li barely heard anything about it over the past two years.

In February last year, she received a letter from a coroner confirming that the cause of death was a gunshot wound to the chest.
In early April, she wrote to the court to inquire about a death inquest.
In response, the court said police had been instructed to produce a death investigation report, and a decision on whether to hold an inquest would be made after receiving the complete report.
Since then, she has called the Coroner’s Court general hotline every month to check on the progress, only to be told: “The investigation is still under way.”
On the other hand, she stopped contacting police after the contact person who treated her kindly retired.
Only an officer from the Complaints Against Police Office continued to check on her regularly, but declined to reveal details of their investigation.
“Every step has been very hard for me … I’m always afraid that something bad will happen to me and no one will be left to follow up on my husband’s case,” she said. “I hope everything can go faster.”
In the first few months after her husband’s death, she was unable to eat and sleep well, losing over 20 pounds (9kg) in just one month.
Now, she suffers from a failing memory, slowed reaction times and wakes up repeatedly throughout the night.
Whenever she has a moment to herself, the memory of her husband covered in blood and surrounded by police after being shot floods back into her mind.
“I deeply regret calling police. I made a call, and then he died … I will not forgive myself for the rest of my life,” she said.
“My intention was simply to have my husband taken to hospital, as we did before.”
She questioned why officers discharged a fatal shot to the chest rather than retreating down the stairwell or deploying non-lethal options such as pepper spray and shields.

In response to the South China Morning Post queries, police said they submitted the investigation report to the Coroner’s Court in June 2025.
The court requested further information, which was provided this month, and police were waiting for further instructions from the court.
As for the complaint filed with police, it is being handled in a “fair and impartial manner in accordance with established procedures”.
The judiciary declined to comment on individual cases.
It said the coroner would decide whether to hold an inquest after reviewing the report, and police might be directed to conduct further investigations if needed, with the deceased’s next of kin to be updated on the progress and decision on the inquest.
Under Practice Direction 39 on coronial procedures, which took effect in June last year, if an investigation is not completed within nine months of the date of the interim report, or if no decision whether to hold an inquest has been made, the court will, where appropriate, update the family every three months on the reasons for the delay – which did not happen in Mrs Li’s case.
The guidelines do not set a fixed deadline for supplying supplementary information once a report is submitted.
Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a community organiser at the Society for Community Organisation who helped Mrs Li, said he believed that the case would rely on expert assessment of firearms use and police protocols to evaluate whether the officer’s actions were justified.
“Without disclosing anything, families are left in this situation – with just one letter on hand and they have to reach out repeatedly in anxiety,” he said.
“Even after the report is submitted, it takes time for the pre-inquest [reviews] to be scheduled before the formal hearing; more waiting is anticipated.”

Delays of two to three years before a coroner’s inquest opens are not uncommon in Hong Kong, according to lawyer Jonathan Man Ho-ching.
Man said police handled death investigations alongside routine work without a dedicated unit, according to his understanding.
There are only three designated coroners in Hong Kong handling inquests while performing regular duties such as granting burial and autopsy orders, with their workload further compounded following major disasters such as the Wang Fuk Court fire that claimed 168 lives.
The primary recourse for families is to query the Coroner’s Court directly regarding the progress of their case.
“Just like any case, the longer a death inquest is delayed, the less ideal it is because witnesses might not be able to remember details, or might simply be unreachable any more, as seen during the Lamma ferry disaster inquests,” Man said.
“A wait is often inevitable … which is very hard on families because an inquest allows them to understand what happened to their loved ones, providing closure and helping them move on.”
Man said he believed Hong Kong could do better in strengthening communication with bereaved families during these prolonged periods.
“In some jurisdictions, death inquiries are not treated purely as a legal procedure; caseworkers are assigned to families to help them navigate the process,” he said.

data.title: Exclusive|Hong Kong’s next policy address is just around the corner. Here’s what to expect
data.description:
Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu’s coming policy address will introduce measures to remove hurdles for businesses setting up shop in the Northern Metropolis and include proactive initiatives to strengthen innovation hubs, research efforts and tech applications, the South China Morning Post has learned.
Government sources said measures supporting the megaproject in the northern New Territories and backing innovation were expected to be major highlights of the chief executive’s policy address on Wednesday – the same day he will unveil the city’s first five-year plan.
The SCMP also learned that Lee’s coming speech would last no more than three hours and be equally split between the five-year plan and the policy address.
The five-year plan is expected to include aspirational and binding key performance indicators and goals. The latter will cover concrete targets for both the incumbent and future administrations.
“The new policy address will feature a number of deregulation and streamlining measures,” one insider said.
“The government will further streamline development procedures and facilitate business operations, including relaxing rules in various commercial and operational sectors to unlock market vitality.”
The source said that, given the Northern Metropolis was considered a key testing ground, authorities were determined to remove red tape and scrap certain rules to help speed things up.
But he added that the government would also work to safeguard urban planning, environmental protection and safety measures.
A second source said streamlining the process for obtaining approvals from various departments during construction was one direction. “Cutting time means cutting costs for companies,” the insider said.

The planned megaproject includes several innovation hubs and a university town, comprises 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) and aims to diversify the economy through technology.
It is also expected to create more demand for skilled jobs and learning opportunities for young people, while offering larger homes for a better quality of life.
A third insider said that more details, including the fixed sizes of land plots for the three university town areas and the latest timeline for completing various infrastructure projects, such as new rail lines, would be covered in the policy address.
The insider added that authorities were expected to increase the number of research postgraduate and doctoral places funded by the University Grants Committee, to help support local universities’ expansion into the Northern Metropolis.
The first source also said Lee would announce more proactive policies to boost industrial development, reinforcing the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster’s status as a world-leading hub.
Last week, the World Intellectual Property Organisation ranked the cluster first globally.
The source also touched on how Hong Kong planned to develop synergy among three of its own innovation parks, as well as fostering collaboration among five other research and development (R&D) institutes to expand the city’s research capabilities.
“The three major innovation and technology hubs will form a ‘North-Central-South’ spatial strategy, centred on the Hetao Hong Kong Park in the north, the Hong Kong Science Park system in the middle and Cyberport in the south,” the source said.
“Building on existing research capabilities, the five major R&D institutes will further strategically expand into key domains such as microelectronics, artificial intelligence, and life and health sciences, forming an integrated ecosystem spanning education, technology, talent, industry and capital.”

The five institutes are the Hong Kong Productivity Council, the Hong Kong Applied Science and Technology Research Institute, the Hong Kong Microelectronics Research and Development Institute, the Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute, and the Life and Health Technology Research Institute.
The second source said one option for authorities was to invite smaller companies, local universities and organisations from mainland China and the rest of the world to take part in projects at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, the site of the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park.
Such a move could nurture ideas and attract talent, help to sustain the integrated research ecosystem, the source said.
The first source also said the government had plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to develop Hong Kong society. “But authorities will attach great importance to the safety, ethics and responsibilities involved when using AI,” the insider said.
The source added that the government would integrate the technology’s usage across various policy areas such as tourism, welfare, finance and legal services, while introducing the use of robots to communities.
The third insider said authorities would also consider enacting legislation to combat cyber-dependent crimes.
Observers are watching closely to gauge where the last policy address of Lee’s current term and the city’s first five-year plan will take Hong Kong, and whether such high-level strategic planning will be used by Lee to build momentum for securing a second five-year term next July.




In an opinion piece published in the SCMP on Monday, Lee stressed that the five-year plan would not change Hong Kong’s capitalist system but instead fully exploit its advantages to map the city’s long-term development.
This would ultimately “enable citizens to flourish” by creating jobs and upward mobility, the city leader wrote.
“I want the people of Hong Kong – every one of you – to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment,” he added.
Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, called for greater flexibility in investment models for the Northern Metropolis, including more flexible arrangements for land payments.
He also proposed new approaches, such as allowing joint development between the private sector and the industrial park operators.
Lo urged the government to publish a list of the industries it expected to develop in the megaproject, along with corresponding plans and a clear timetable, to give the business community greater certainty and enable better evaluation of economic gains.
“People may still lack an understanding of the detailed planning of the Northern Metropolis. More promotion is needed in this area,” Lo said.
“If [the business community] knows what stage of development will be reached by a certain year, that will allow us to make better plans.”
Leonard Chan Tik-yuen, founding chairman of the Hong Kong Innovative Technology Development Association, said he expected the government to relax regulations on the testing of advanced driverless vehicles and drones in the Northern Metropolis, noting that some trials were difficult to conduct in urban areas.
He also called for better cross-border flow of data, specimens and equipment, describing it as a unique advantage for the city.
He added that the administration must clearly define the positioning of the three I&T clusters under the North-Central-South strategy and ensure proper coordination to avoid homogenisation and internal competition.

data.title: Hong Kong district councillor remanded in custody after underage sex conviction
data.description:
A Hong Kong court has remanded a district councillor in custody pending sentence after convicting him of unlawful sex with a 13-year-old girl 15 years ago, rejecting his claim that the allegation was politically motivated.
Yuen Long District Council member Sei Chun-hing, 39, is set to become the first elected officer to face imprisonment for a criminal offence since a Beijing-led electoral overhaul in 2021, which ensured only those endorsed by authorities as “patriotic” can assume public office.
The District Court on Monday accepted the complainant’s testimony that Sei had committed sexual acts on her on March 14, 2011, telling her he expected the then secondary school pupil to reciprocate a month after he gave her a handcrafted Valentine’s Day gift.
Sei, a personal assistant to former cultural and sports lawmaker Ma Fung-kwok, was convicted of unlawful sex with a girl under 16, an offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment.
He was acquitted of a separate indecent assault charge relating to a 2008 incident on technical grounds.
Judge Stanley Chan Kwong-chi also dismissed Sei’s contention that the woman’s evidence was tainted by her desire to punish him for his pro-establishment views or for ending their relationship.
The government announced an internal inquiry following a petition by the Yuen Long District Council chairman and three other members to the secretary for home and youth affairs.
“The government places great importance on the conduct and integrity of [district council] members, and will closely monitor the progress of the legal proceedings and follow up accordingly,” a spokesman said.
The complainant, now 29 and identified only as X, said she was 11 years old and in Primary Six when Sei, then an assistant to the director of her school’s theatre production, molested her in November 2008.
She said she avoided contact with the defendant after the incident until they met again in October 2010, reconciled and soon became a couple.
The woman recalled Sei, who was 23 at the time, describing her as his wife and suggesting she could only demonstrate her love by having sex with him.
On Valentine’s Day in 2011, Sei gave her a rose-shaped ornament engraved with their names and asked her to reciprocate a month later on White Day, usually celebrated as a second Valentine’s Day in East Asia.
The complainant said she reluctantly had sex with the accused at his residence in Tin Shui Wai to maintain their relationship.
In the witness box, Sei admitted developing romantic feelings for the girl but dismissed her allegations as pure fabrication.
He insisted he met the girl for the first time a month after the alleged sexual assault in 2008, while contending he could not have had sex with the complainant at his home in 2011 because he was busy with work.
Judge Chan rejected Sei’s account as untruthful, noting that metadata attached to images he submitted as evidence might have been altered to aid his defence.
He stressed that the complainant’s motive for filing the police report was not pivotal to the court’s determination.
“The alleged incidents of indecent assault and unlawful sex, if proven beyond reasonable doubt, are facts independent of whether X had filed a police report for political reasons or because her love had turned to hate,” he said.
The judge said the complainant gave a credible and reasonable account of the event that took place on March 14, 2011, while rejecting the defendant’s claim that he was at a meeting with a theatre colleague that afternoon.
Chan further held that he molested the woman when she was 11 in 2008 but said the prosecution failed to prove its case because the complainant was unable to show the incident took place at the time and place specified in the indictment.
The court will hear oral mitigation arguments on October 27 before passing sentence.
Under the District Councils Ordinance, a member is disqualified if sentenced to more than three months’ imprisonment for an offence.
Additionally, performance monitoring guidelines mandated by the government stipulate that an officeholder can face sanctions for gross misconduct or a criminal offence attracting a jail term, even if the sentence is not severe enough to warrant disqualification.

data.title: Foundation collects tributes to Hong Kong’s Tung Chee-hwa for online memorial
data.description:
The China-United States Exchange Foundation has launched a permanent tribute webpage to Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, and collected more than 100 reflections from political and business heavyweights around the world.
The foundation, established by Tung in 2008, said the webpage, which launched on Monday, included tributes from Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus and Max Baucus, former United States ambassador to China.
“This permanent tribute not only placemarks his remarkable record of public service but honours his lifelong belief that dialogue can advance global peace, progress and prosperity,” foundation president James Chau said.
“Above all, this tribute is intended to inspire a new generation to advance the cause to which Mr Tung was deeply devoted,” he said. “I saw first-hand Mr Tung’s exceptional sense of duty, generosity and conviction.”
Among those who contributed to the memorial was Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Emeritus Senior Minister Goh Chok Tong of the city state.
Goh said his friendship with Tung went back to the early 1970s when they were both in the shipping industry.
“I will remember him as a helpful, sincere, trustworthy friend whom I had the privilege of knowing for more than half a century,” he said.
Yunus said Tung’s life was one of quiet but determined service, highlighting how he guided Hong Kong through a historic and difficult transition as well as building understanding and trust between China and the US.
“That kind of patient, long-term bridge-building is rare, and it leaves a lasting mark far beyond the institutions he led,” he said.

Others who paid tribute to Tung included former US treasury secretary Hank Paulson; John Podesta, former White House chief of staff for Bill Clinton; and retired US admiral William Owens.
“He was the epitome of a citizen diplomat. Despite strong differences between our systems and our governments, [Tung] had an unshakeable belief that the people of China and the people of the US had much in common and could share a prosperous and peaceful future through dialogue and understanding,” Podesta said.
Mogens Lykketoft, a past president of the United Nations General Assembly, former World Health Organization director general Margaret Chan Fung Fu-chun and Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai also paid tribute to Tung on the website. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
The tribute page also has a dedicated space where the public can share their own memories and reflections.
Tung, who died on September 8 at the age of 89, is remembered for a tenure marked by difficult policy choices and successive crises, with former officials saying some of his past decisions had taken on a different significance with the passage of time.
He largely withdrew from public view in his final years and was last seen publicly in July 2021, when he attended the premiere of a film marking the centenary of the founding of the Communist Party of China.

data.title: Man arrested over alleged HK$2.8 million Hong Kong school admission scam
data.description:
A man has been arrested for allegedly defrauding an education consultant of nearly HK$3 million (US$382,500) by claiming he could secure dozens of places at a Hong Kong school, the South China Morning Post has learned.
A police source said on Monday that the suspect, a 51-year-old Hongkonger, who claimed to be a businessman, signed a contract with a woman education consultant, 45, on March 1, 2024, promising to provide dozens of places at a school called “Kiangsu-Chekiang College”.
Believing the claims, the consultant transferred about HK$2.84 million in 23 instalments between April and July 2024 to his mainland Chinese bank account, covering application fees for 37 students, the source added.
He had allegedly promised access to 50 secondary school places at the college, assuring her that her students would also be given guaranteed entry into universities in Hong Kong or Macau regardless of their Diploma of Secondary Education results.
However, the source said none of the students received admission offers from the school or any higher education institution. He subsequently cut off contact, prompting the woman to file a police report in May this year.
Investigators intercepted him at Hong Kong airport on July 29 this year as he attempted to leave the city.
He was arrested on suspicion of fraud.

There are three secondary schools and one primary school carrying the “Kiangsu‑Chekiang” name in Hong Kong. The three secondary schools are located in Sha Tin, Kwai Chung and North Point.
The one in North Point, Kiangsu-Chekiang College, is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents.
The primary school, the Kiangsu and Chekiang Primary School, is also in North Point.
Kiangsu-Chekiang College in North Point is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents.

data.title: Big Macs from above: Meituan and McDonald’s launch drone delivery in Shanghai
data.description:
Shanghai’s bustling riverfront has become the latest testing ground for urban logistics technology, with McDonald’s and Chinese food-delivery giant Meituan joining forces to launch the country’s first catering brand-exclusive drone-delivery route.
Commencing operations last week, the new service allows visitors strolling or exercising along the scenic West Bund area in Shanghai’s Xuhui district to have their fast-food orders ‘airdropped’ directly to designated kiosks, according to a recent statement by district authorities.
The 3.1km (1.93-mile) flight path, originating from a McDonald’s restaurant in Xuhui, is designed to serve thousands of office workers in the area, as well as the large crowds of tourists who frequent the riverside, the statement said.
The customised drones can handle a maximum payload of 2.4kg (5.29lbs) and complete waterfront deliveries in as fast as 10 minutes, according to an official Meituan statement.
The move reflects how China is doubling down on its so-called “low-altitude economy” as a new engine for tech innovation. The Shanghai route offers a glimpse into how airborne logistics can play an increasing role in the fiercely competitive food delivery industry.

Meituan has been expanding its drone business in recent years, seeking to maintain an early-mover advantage over domestic competitors like Alibaba Group Holding and JD.com in the race to dominate next-generation urban logistics. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Meituan’s commercial drone delivery orders have surpassed 900,000, the company told Chinese media in May. Meituan is likely to see its drone business achieve large-scale “front-end profitability” in the next two to three years, Meituan vice-president Mao Yinian was quoted as saying.
The new route is part of a broader “aerial delivery network” planned by Meituan to connect landmarks in Xuhui. It also marks the food-delivery giant’s second “systematic urban aerial network”, following its first in Shenzhen. The Shanghai network hosts nearly 20 catering brands, and Meituan said it expects that number to surpass 40 by the end of the year.
Wei Qijun, who is in charge of national commercial management for Meituan’s drones, was cited by the district government as saying that the aircraft maintained a “99.999 per cent safety factor” – a metric he attributed to the company’s nine years of research and testing.
The drones can operate normally in moderate rain and snow, as well as in Force 6 winds, Wei said. On the Beaufort scale, Force 6 indicates strong winds of up to 49km/h (31mph). Wei added that the system would automatically ground the fleet, after completing active orders, if the weather turned extreme.

data.title: Hong Kong urged to overhaul ecotourism planning and expand bookings for hotspots
data.description:
Hong Kong should overhaul its ecotourism planning and allow visitors to book ahead at more of its popular countryside attractions, a lawmaker has said, after a survey found most residents believed the city had strong potential for nature-focused experiences but lacked enough quality options.
A poll of 651 residents commissioned by lawmaker Perry Yiu Pak-leung’s office and think tank New Youth Forum found 71.8 per cent agreed Hong Kong’s countryside resources could be developed into high-quality ecotourism products.
But the same proportion said most visitors heading to the countryside were merely taking part in ordinary leisure activities rather than “genuine” ecotourism.
“Hong Kong has very rich ecotourism resources, but unfortunately we have not made good use of them for a long time,” Yiu said.
The survey, conducted by telephone between August 18 and 26, also found that 62.1 per cent of respondents felt the city lacked enough high-quality ecotourism products, while 59 per cent said they would be interested in taking part in more in-depth experiences.
About 83.3 per cent agreed quality ecotourism should combine professional guiding, conservation education and sustainable development.
Regarding visitor management, 75.8 per cent supported booking systems at popular ecological attractions, while 73.1 per cent said selected hotspots should be accessible only through accredited travel agencies and professional guides.

Yiu, who represents the tourism sector in the Legislative Council, said the government should move away from what he described as a “passive, piecemeal and firefighting” approach to managing popular attractions and instead adopt a strategy based on policy coordination, capacity management and industry accreditation.
He called for a high-level cross-departmental task force to oversee ecotourism development, saying the existing interdepartmental mechanism used to handle crowds during major holidays was insufficient for long-term planning.
He highlighted that managing overtourism at the High Island Reservoir East Dam in Sai Kung alone required the involvement of the Transport Department, Tourism Commission, Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, Water Supplies Department, police and district authorities.
Yiu suggested the government review the booking trial at the High Island East Dam and Po Pin Chau before considering extending similar arrangements to other popular sites.
He cited Tai Mo Shan as one area that could come under pressure as authorities promote the “four peaks” green tourism initiative, which also covers The Peak, Lantau Peak and Sai Kung Hoi.
Yiu noted the High Island reservation scheme had recorded a no-show rate of about 41 per cent over its first two weekends, but argued unused slots could be opened to walk-in visitors and that frontline staff should retain flexibility in managing entry times.
Travel Industry Council chairman Tommy Tam Kwong-shun emphasised that crowd control is only the first step, arguing that ecologically sensitive or heavily visited sites should eventually be managed by accredited travel agencies and professionally trained guides.
“If we genuinely want to achieve professional guiding, conservation education and sustainable development together, the government should consider allowing accredited professional travel agencies and guides to coordinate visits to designated ecologically sensitive and popular attractions,” Tam said.
He also called for a dedicated accreditation system for eco-tour operators and guides, saying professionally trained operators could provide visitors with richer experiences.
Additionally, Tam urged the Travel Industry Authority to strengthen online patrols of social media platforms, including RedNote, to target unlicensed cross-border tour operations at source.
Derek Tse Yue-tak, general manager of Eco Travel, said transport restrictions and cumbersome permit procedures were making it harder for operators to develop quality countryside products.
He also said unlicensed cross-border hiking tours organised by guides from mainland China had increasingly eaten into the business of licensed local operators.

data.title: Hong Kong to sweeten school merger deals, offer housing measures to lift births
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities are expected to provide more incentives to encourage under-enrolled public schools to merge to survive, while announcing housing measures and tax reductions to tackle the falling birth rate in this week’s policy address, the South China Morning Post has learned.
A government source told the South China Morning Post that the policy address by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday would offer additional incentives to encourage the merger of subsidised schools amid the shrinking student population.
Currently, if a primary school merges with another institution to allow the affected pupils to continue their studies, a one-off allowance of HK$1 million (US$127,500) will be granted to cover additional expenses.
In March, the Education Bureau announced that a record 15 primary schools would not be allowed to operate subsidised Primary One classes for this academic year because they had failed to secure at least 16 pupils.
Among them, eight chose to merge with other schools – which is the most popular option – while four chose to close down after three years, and two opted to operate private Primary One classes. The remaining school is already in the process of merging with another institution.
The survival challenge of primary schools is expected to become more serious, as the number of babies born from 2021 to 2025, who will be entering Primary One in the coming years, keeps declining and hit a record low last year.
The Education Bureau even expects the number of six-year-olds will stand at only 31,500 in 2029, a 16 per cent drop from 37,600 Primary One pupils in public schools this school year.
Jessie Cheung Chok-fong, a consultant at the Subsidised Primary Schools Council and a primary school principal, said schools generally used the current allowance to cover pupils’ extra expenses incurred by the mergers.
“If a school in one district merges with a school in another district, schools have to offer school buses for students to commute, and parents will also be given money to buy a new set of textbooks and school uniforms after joining the new school,” she said.
“More resources are definitely good for schools planning to merge, but schools always look at how much they are given before spending.”
At present, secondary schools that continue to operate Form One classes after a merger will be provided with a one-off allowance of HK$500,000 for each merging level to cover the additional expenses.
Over the past few years, only four government secondary schools and two secondary schools operated by Caritas Hong Kong have chosen the merger option.
The issue of a declining number of Secondary One students is not as imminent as it is for the primary section, as the local number of births started to fall in 2017.
Secondary schools now have to secure 29 students to operate two Form One classes, or they will face survival risks.

The source said the policy address would also try to boost the birth rate by offering tax incentives and rolling out housing measures, as authorities wanted to avoid depending solely on cash giveaways for families.
Last month, Hong Kong recorded 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026, down 15.6 per cent from the 35,200 recorded during the same period a year earlier – a record low.
The decline in births came despite the government’s introduction of a “baby bonus” scheme in 2023, offering a one-off HK$20,000 cash award to new parents to encourage families to have children.
The scheme was planned for an initial three years.
In June, city leader Lee said the Hong Kong government would conduct a consultation on its slew of pro-baby incentives amid persistently low birth rates, noting that delayed marriage and cultural shifts were limiting the effectiveness of such policies.
He conceded that delayed marriage, driven by career pursuits and postgraduate education becoming more common, had disincentivised couples from having children.
The median age for first marriage among Hongkongers rose from 31.2 for men and 29.3 for women in 2015 to 32.6 and 31, respectively, in 2025.
He also pointed to changing cultural values, including the decline of the traditional view that children serve as an old-age safeguard and the growing prioritisation of individual aspirations.

data.title: Syndicate dispute or theft? The legal fight over HK$30 million Mark Six prize
data.description:
A group of 14 government employees can only recover their shares of a HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) Mark Six windfall through civil legal proceedings after a colleague allegedly refused to split the prize and disappeared, a lawyer has said.
Vitus Lawyers principal partner Vitus Leung Wing-hang told the South China Morning Post on Monday that retrieving the money would not be easy for the victims, who work at the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department office.
Leung added that the 36-year-old colleague, arrested on Friday on suspicion of theft, would still face criminal charges even if he returned the disputed funds.
“If that person is found guilty, the bank account doesn’t belong to the other 14 people. So the bank will not release the money immediately. We have to go to civil court,” he said.
The dispute centres on the suspect’s failure to reach a consensus with the 14 victims over his claim to a larger share of the windfall. He reportedly argued he deserved more because he bought the tickets, even though all 15 had contributed to a pooled fund.
The group won the prize in the September 5 draw, part of the record HK$228 million “snowball” jackpot marking the 50th anniversary of Mark Six, organised by the Hong Kong Jockey Club.
After a deadlock in a meeting over how to split the prize, the man reportedly vanished from work for five days.
His disappearance prompted a 53-year-old colleague to file a police report, leading to the 36-year-old man’s arrest on Friday for alleged theft.

Police froze the suspect’s bank account and the HK$30 million windfall pending further investigation.
Leung said the victims could not simply ask the bank to hand over the money even if the suspect were convicted of theft.
The bank would not release the funds immediately because the frozen account belonged to the suspect and might also contain his personal cash mixed with the prize money, he said.
He compared the civil recovery process with online fraud cases, in which victims who had deposited money into a third party’s bank account had to sue to get it back.
The group would need to hire lawyers to initiate civil proceedings to recover their shares, which are now held in a police-frozen account, Leung said.
“They apply for the money to be released to them, and also the bank account could contain monies more than that amount to be released to the 14 people, right?” Leung added.
“Because that person could have his own amount, own cash, own money in the bank account. So we need another civil procedure to get the money back.”
In the suspect’s case, possession of a copy of a winning lottery ticket did not necessarily equate to full legal ownership of the prize money, Leung said.
He said the law carefully distinguished between the person holding the ticket and the true beneficial owners of the asset.
Although the arrested man held the ticket and the funds in his bank account, he and the other 14 contributors remained the beneficial owners, he added.
With any property, including land, the legal title might be in one person’s name, but the beneficial owner could be someone else, Leung said.
He also said that to avoid disputes, participants in lottery syndicates should establish clear terms before purchasing a ticket.
He recommended keeping a basic written record.
“Then we can just put it in a simple message in the WhatsApp group,” Leung said.

data.title: A ploy to entrench US lead? China pushes back on calls for slowdown in AI
data.description:
Calls by US tech leaders for a voluntary slowdown in artificial intelligence development have run into sharp pushback from Chinese researchers and state media, who question whether the proposal is a genuine push for responsibility or an effort to entrench America’s technological lead.
The debate intensified on Monday when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined a growing chorus of Silicon Valley leaders demanding industry-wide “pacing”, warning that competitive pressure must not override safety as AI advanced rapidly.
“The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened,” Altman wrote on social media platform X.
“Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.”
His comments followed a call on Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for frontier labs to slow down development of their most powerful models – a stance also endorsed by xAI founder Elon Musk.
In a post on his personal website, Amodei also called for “worldwide pacing of the frontier”, but admitted this would be “much harder to achieve.”
“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” he said.

Industry leaders and observers are urging a slowdown in AI development after a series of recent safety incidents where experimental models in testing phases hacked into real-world systems.
In China, however, the sudden pivot towards self-imposed restraint has been met with scepticism. Some Chinese researchers argued that a blanket slowdown disproportionately protects established US incumbents while freezing latecomers out of the market.
“Those who already possess resources can afford a pause. Those who are still building their careers cannot,” said Zhang Xuanming, a researcher with Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen team, in an article on X on Friday.
For market leaders, a slowdown was a precaution; for rising players, a “blanket pause” threatened to “close the frontier” before they could compete, he wrote. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
Other Chinese engineers echoed that frustration.
“When we try to accelerate you tell me to slow down? OMG [oh my God] …” Lin Junyang, a former lead researcher on Alibaba’s Qwen models, wrote in an X post on Sunday, calling on US executives to “stop pretending” they needed permission to operate.
Ronny He, an engineer at Shanghai-based AI firm MiniMax, wrote on social media on Sunday, “Yesterday, the mission was AGI. Today, we’re told to slow down. Why do you always get to define the game – and change the rules?”
AGI, or artificial general intelligence, refers to software that matches human-level reasoning across a variety of tasks.
Concerns have also surfaced in Chinese state media. In a commentary on Sunday, state-owned tabloid Global Times accused Anthropic’s Amodei of proposing a “quiet AI Cold War” to widen America’s technological lead “through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies” while excluding China from global AI governance.

In his essay, Amodei called on Washington to tighten restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, while cracking down on “distillation” – using AI outputs from more advanced models to train cheaper rival models – and the theft of proprietary “model weights”, the underlying code and data that power AI systems.
“If we execute these measures well, I believe they would slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next three to five years,” Amodei wrote.
Beijing and Washington push ahead
The call for caution faces resistance not only in China, but also from the White House.
US President Donald Trump dismissed calls for a pause over the weekend, warning that halting progress risks ceding America’s technological edge to China. “Whoever wins with AI wins,” Trump told reporters, writing off safety concerns as the work of “negative forces”.
Meanwhile, Beijing is framing AI as a key national security domain. Writing in a journal published by the Cyberspace Administration of China on Sunday, state security minister Chen Yixin labelled AI a primary arena for superpower rivalry, urging robust security frameworks and global governance to manage rising threats.
Rather than slowing down, Chinese AI players are accelerating their development timelines.
Z.ai, known in China as Zhipu AI, said on Sunday it had raised 33.5 billion yuan (US$5 billion), earmarking 60 per cent of the funds to develop its next-generation GLM model and advance a “fully self-training” system.
Last week, prominent researchers – including Zhou Bowen, head of the Shanghai AI Lab, alongside engineers from ByteDance – submitted a paper outlining a five-stage road map towards systems capable of autonomously improving their own code.

data.title: Hong Kong’s HK$500b silver economy by 2034 offers ‘ocean’ of prospects: Paul Chan
data.description:
Hong Kong’s silver economy is set to become a HK$500 billion (US$63.8 billion) market by 2034, the city’s finance chief has said, urging the elderly care industry to deploy technology and explore cross-border opportunities.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Monday that Hong Kong’s ageing population presented both a challenge and a “promising blue ocean” market opportunity for the city, which could serve as a model for other regions.
In his speech at the 30th anniversary of the Senior Citizen Home Safety Association (SCHSA), Chan noted that the expenditure by individuals aged 60 and above in Hong Kong could grow by 47 per cent from around HK$340 billion in 2024 to nearly HK$500 billion by 2034.
“The growth of the silver economy is not merely about increasing products and services, but also about offering better lifestyle choices for seniors with different capabilities and needs,” Chan said.
He said that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) had enabled innovative applications in elderly care services, including medical diagnosis and daily living care, while robots could share the load of household chores and assist with physical tasks such as patient transfers.
“The direction of using technology to boost caregiving efficiency and relieve carer burden is very clear, and Hong Kong has the right conditions to take the lead in this field,” he said.
The city had advantages – including world-class life and health research capabilities, a concentration of funding, talent and start-ups – and was building an international medical innovation centre, Chan said.
“The key is to connect these strengths to propel research outcomes into practical and commercially sustainable services,” he said.
The Greater Bay Area also offered new opportunities as new demands had emerged for care service referrals, health information sharing and cross-boundary support arrangements, Chan noted.
“If we can establish a safe, reliable and seamless service model, there will be opportunities to replicate and promote this model to benefit more seniors,” he said.
“This may well be a promising blue ocean worth exploring.”

At the same event, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the city had become a “super-aged society” as the median age of Hong Kong’s population was currently 49 years, with nearly a quarter of the population aged 65 or above.
Sun said the government’s promotion of senior-friendly technology had raised public awareness and attracted more investment through the HK$2 billion Innovation and Technology Fund for Application in Elderly and Rehabilitation Care.
He added that gerontechnology would advance rapidly in the next five years and that it was crucial to cultivate seniors to learn and use it as early as possible, but authorities had to tackle cost and privacy issues.
“Another issue the government needs to address is the legal concerns of the public, including how to resolve privacy issues at home and how to ensure that data does not stray from its proper scope,” he said.
Joyce Ho Mei-yee, tech enablement director at the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, said the city could consider importing gerontechnology products developed in mainland China, which offered high cost-performance advantages.
“Bringing mainland products to Hong Kong involves localisation, which is adapting technology and language for our elderly users,” she said during a panel discussion.
However, Ho said popularising these products would be a major challenge moving forward as the localisation process was difficult.
Law Chi-kwong, former chairman of the SCHSA, said he expected future developments in gerontechnology to proceed at double the speed compared with the past.
His association introduced the Emergency Alarm System three decades ago when 30 elderly died during a cold spell at Chinese New Year. Elderly living alone could press a button and call a 24-hour support system for immediate help.
Law said he envisioned the system growing into an intelligent robot which could see and move in the future.
“This kind of service will integrate various aspects of care and companionship with robotics,” he said.
“Technology is neutral, but the question is how we design the service to achieve a ‘human-centric’ approach, keeping genuine care at the very core of the service.”

data.title: Forms Syntron draws Hong Kong’s next-gen tycoons in HK$940 million IPO
data.description:
Hong Kong’s younger generation of tycoons is becoming increasingly active in the city’s initial public offering market through family offices and private investments. But their investments extend beyond the property and traditional financial sectors associated with their predecessors, into technology and digital finance.
Prominent business leaders Cheng Chi-heng of New World Development and Peter Lee Ka-kit of Henderson Land participated as cornerstone investors in Shenzhen Forms Syntron Information’s HK$940 million (US$119.8 million) Hong Kong listing, according to the company’s official filing on Monday.
In exchange for guaranteed share allocations and a mandatory commitment to hold the stocks for at least six months, Cheng and Lee agreed to buy HK$40 million and HK$39.6 million worth of shares, respectively. They were joined by private investment firm Thalassa Capital and Hong Kong-listed LCD manufacturer Yeebo International Holdings.
Lee has been particularly active in Hong Kong’s IPO market in recent years. Through his wholly-owned private investment vehicle, he has served as a cornerstone investor in several high-profile debuts, including XtalPi in 2024 – the first specialist technology company to list under Hong Kong’s Chapter 18C rules designed for innovative firms in hi-tech industries.
As the city’s broader IPO market stages a robust recovery in 2026 – with total funds raised surpassing HK$340 billion in the first eight months – tycoons and family offices are drawing renewed market attention.
Forms Syntron said it met these high-profile investors through business connections, introductions by corporate partners and global offering underwriters during its regular business and investment activities.
The financial technology service provider, which caters to the banking industry, has started taking investor orders for its Hong Kong listing and expects its trading debut on September 22. It is offering 58.9 million shares at a maximum price of HK$16 each, according to its listing document. The price marks a 40 per cent discount compared with the 23.02 yuan (US$3.43) closing price of its Shenzhen-listed shares on Friday.
The company plans to channel the capital raised into research and development, operational capabilities over the next three to five years, international sales expansion across mainland China and overseas markets, and potential strategic technology acquisitions.
Although headquartered in mainland China and already listed in the A-share market, Forms Syntron has strong ties to Hong Kong. Founder and chairman Chow Chi Kwan grew up and was educated in the city, earning a bachelor’s degree in social science from the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 1995. He also serves as a non-official member of Hong Kong’s Digital Economy Development Committee.
Founded in 2003, Forms Syntron provides fintech software development, consulting and systems integration services to banks, regulatory authorities and financial institutions across mainland China and Hong Kong, supporting their digital transformation.
The Hong Kong market now accounts for more than 80 per cent of the company’s total revenue. Its client base mainly comprises financial institutions and non-bank financial firms, with its top five customers contributing 89.1 per cent of revenue in 2025.
The company recorded revenue of 630 million yuan (US$93.9 million) last year, down from 740 million yuan in 2024. Full-year net profit rose 10.3 per cent year on year to 74 million yuan. The company won 221 new projects in 2025, compared with 297 in 2024.

data.title: Hong Kong’s iPhone scam: how to shop safely online and prevent credit card fraud
data.description:
More than 700 Hongkongers were shocked to discover that their credit cards had been used to place unauthorised orders for Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro series handsets over the weekend.
Although banks reassured victims they would not be charged as long as the cards were used with due care and the transactions were proven to be unauthorised, the incident still caused widespread concern over credit card security.
The South China Morning Post asked information technology experts for practical tips on how to safeguard credit cards.
1. What happened?
Over the weekend, many social media users in Hong Kong reported that their credit cards had been compromised to place orders for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro series, which opened for pre-order on Saturday evening.
Police confirmed receiving over 700 reports involving HK$14.7 million (US$1.87 million) in unauthorised transactions.
Experts and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) suggested that multiple-factor authentication might have been disabled by Apple to facilitate a smoother customer experience amid a surge in orders, creating a loophole for scammers to exploit.
Major Hong Kong banks said victims would not be held liable, provided the transactions were proven unauthorised and cardholders acted with due care.
Meanwhile, Apple said it was reviewing all its current orders to identify and cancel suspicious transactions.


2. What is 3D Secure?
3D Secure (3DS) serves as an extra security layer for online payments that helps authenticate the buyer’s identity.
It is used by major credit card organisations, including Visa, Mastercard, American Express and UnionPay.
With the latest version of 3DS, card issuers can determine transaction risks using information provided by the merchant, browser fingerprinting, and the user’s transaction history.
While most legitimate transactions are completed seamlessly without requiring customer action, higher-risk purchases may prompt buyers to enter a one-time password (OTP) or approve the transaction via their mobile banking app.
However, some merchants opt to disable 3DS through their payment gateways to streamline the checkout process.
According to the HKMA, when merchants bypass 3DS authentication, they must bear full financial liability for any losses resulting from unauthorised transactions.
3. How was the credit card information exposed?
Experts who spoke to SCMP believe the stolen credit card information had been leaked previously and held by fraudsters over time.
The data was likely compromised during purchases on retail websites that were not obliged to submit regular audit reports to authorities, and therefore might not constantly review their security features, they added.
“It is common for these retailers – or their processing platforms – to skip encryption when backing up the data. That is exactly how data leaks happen,” said Anthony Lai Cheuk-tung, director of cybersecurity firm VX Research.
Even if the data was encrypted during transmission, that protection might still be dropped when it reaches the database or is shared with contractors for maintenance, leading to risks of breaches, he added.
Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, suspected some victims might have also used proxy purchasing services on concert ticket platforms, where users hand over full payment credentials to automated tools or agents to secure high-demand tickets.
